sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Día de la Nación Charrúa y de la Identidad Indígena
sources.note: Web section “Arqueología,” paragraphs and bullet list at lines 41 to 52: numerous Indigenous groups, mounds, ceramics, domesticated dogs, beans, squash, maize, and native plants.

sources.title: Diego Bracco, Nuestro pasado indígena 4: Los charrúas
sources.note: Museo Nacional de Antropología fascicle, printed and PDF pages 2 to 7: changing territories and named-group distinctions; riverbanks and possible canoes; horse adaptation by about 1640; missions, conflict, alliances, forced transfers, Salsipuedes, and family separation. Dedicated to the overview.

sources.title: Leonel Cabrera Pérez (coord.), Óscar Marozzi, and Jimena Blasco, Fuentes históricas del contacto europeo con los pueblos originarios: siglos XVI–XIX. Manual didáctico para Etnohistoria de la Cuenca del Plata
sources.note: PDF file page 406: Azara reached the Río de la Plata in 1782 and his regional work spans 1781 to 1797; PDF file pages 410 to 412, reproduced-source pages 105 to 108: toldos, meetings, and healer report; PDF file page 432: criticism of Azara’s access and language knowledge.

sources.title: Virginia Bertolotti and Magdalena Coll, Retrato lingüístico del Uruguay: un enfoque histórico sobre las lenguas en la región (2014)
sources.note: PDF file page 101, printed page 101: two Vilardebó manuscripts and their informants; PDF file page 102, printed page 102: November 1842 entry agua hué [we]; PDF file page 103, printed page 103: only a few dozen terms survive and their reliability is low.

sources.title: Olaf Blixen, “Sobre el llamado ‘Complejo Charrúa’,” Boletín del Museo Nacional de Historia Natural 2(28) (1980)
sources.note: Printed pages 1 to 6: no direct observation for the earliest centuries, inconsistent ethnonyms, and the need to combine documentary, archaeological, linguistic, and biological evidence.

sources.title: Erchini and Tobella, Bolas, esferoides y afines: una aproximación en el actual territorio uruguayo
sources.note: Printed pages 75 to 79 and Table 2: 290 objects from 13 departments, possible hunting and fishing uses, manufacturing sequence, poor provenience, and long chronology that prevents easy ethnic assignment.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Patrimonio Arqueológico: Olla cerámica
sources.note: One-page teaching sheet: 18-centimetre coiled pot, soot, residue study, at least 3,000-year regional history, and domestic, ritual, funerary, fish, plant-storage, and fermentation uses.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Probable Colgante lítico
sources.note: One-page teaching sheet: polished slate object from Canelones, traditional pendant interpretation, unknown original function, and sparse regional comparanda.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Cuentas en valvas de moluscos
sources.note: One-page teaching sheet: shell beads from Los Cardos, fracture, percussion, abrasion, drilling, and cautious necklace or clothing interpretation.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología, “Punzón” elaborado en hueso de Venado de Campo
sources.note: One-page teaching sheet: deer-bone awl from Cañada Saldaña, fracture, sawing, abrasion and possible heat hardening, with hide, basketry, and pottery uses.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Patrimonio Arqueológico: Urna funeraria
sources.note: One-page teaching sheet: Isla Larga urn, adult burial, site chronology through the seventeenth century, Tupí-Guaraní or Guaranized attribution, glass beads, and interethnic contact.

sources.title: Suárez and colleagues, New sites and challenges in prehistoric archaeology of Uruguay: recurrent occupations in caves, rockshelters and earthen mounds
sources.note: PDF and journal pages 1 to 2, “Study area and methodology,” and pages 6 to 9, “Results” and “Discussion”: the stratified Tamanduá sequence, lithics, ceramics, burned palm endocarps, historical and roughly 3,000-year-old mound-builder contexts, probable later Guaraní material, and 173 nearby mounds.

sources.title: Admiraal and colleagues, Feasting on fish. Specialized function of pre-colonial pottery of the Cerritos mound builders of southern Brazil
sources.note: PDF and journal pages 2 to 3, archaeological background: scarce and fragmentary human remains limit demographic, dietary, and health reconstruction; pages 7 to 10, “Discussion”: fish and plant residues, with fermentation and seasonal aggregation retained as qualified interpretations.

sources.title: Gazzán and colleagues, From Mounds to Villages: The Social Construction of the Landscape during the Middle and Late Holocene in the India Muerta Lowlands, Uruguay
sources.note: PDF and journal pages 2 to 3, section 1.1: housing and village models, funerary and ceremonial roles, cultivation, mobility, and competing interpretations; pages 13 to 16, section 3.4 plus “Discussion” and “Conclusions”: low flood risk, prominence, visibility, and water-management structures.

sources.title: Bonomo, Politis, and Gianotti, Montículos, jerarquía social y horticultura en las sociedades indígenas del delta del río Paraná
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article abstract and indexed text: Upper Paraná Delta mounds, houses, burials, food evidence, horticulture, and debated hierarchy. Regional evidence only.

sources.title: Silvia Elena Cornero, Lucía Rangone, and Osvaldo Di Sapio, “Identificación de microestructuras y análisis arqueobotánico en sitios del Holoceno tardío de la llanura aluvial del Paraná medio,” Dominguezia 31(1) (2015), 15–21
sources.note: Abstract and printed pages 15 to 21: microremains from adult dental calculus, sediments beneath primary burials, and vessel residues include maize, bean, and squash; the paper situates these finds alongside regional hunting and fishing evidence.

sources.title: Gianotti and colleagues, Knowledge of the Sky among Indigenous Peoples of the South American Lowlands—First Archaeoastronomical Analyses of Orientations at Mounds in Uruguay
sources.note: PDF and journal pages 5 to 12, sections 2 and 3: five mound sets, horizon and axis measurements, roughly 100 observations, and statistical results; pages 17 to 18, “Conclusions”: preliminary relationships to the Southern Cross, Milky Way, and full Moon, with sample limits.

sources.title: Loponte and colleagues, Mortuary pottery and sacred landscapes in complex hunter-gatherers in the Paraná Basin, South America
sources.note: Journal pages 21 to 22, Abstract and “The tubular pottery,” and pages 34 to 38, “Discussion” and “Conclusions”: structural, microscopic, chemical, and residue evidence weighs against domestic use and supports a qualified mortuary interpretation.

sources.title: The genomic prehistory of the Indigenous peoples of Uruguay
sources.note: Article “Introduction,” final two paragraphs and Table 1: two CH2D01-A genomes dated about 1,450 and 668 radiocarbon years BP and caution about historical ethnic labels; “Methods,” subsection “Archaeology and samples”: primary and secondary burials of at least 21 individuals; “Discussion,” final paragraph: limits and needed comparisons.

sources.title: Indigenous Ancestry and Admixture in the Uruguayan Population
sources.note: Article pages 2 to 3, “Introduction” and “Samples and DNA extraction”: ten sequenced volunteers, self-declared ancestries, and the quoted “Charrúa” convention; pages 10 to 13, “Discussion”: small samples and absent Chaná, Minuán, and other adjacent reference groups limit historical identification.

sources.title: Institución Nacional de Derechos Humanos, Paso de Salsipuedes, territorio de la masacre Charrúa
sources.note: Official memory-site account, 15 December 2021: 1831 state massacre, displacement, enslavement, four captives sent to Paris, community petitioners, and 2021 site declaration. Dedicated to ending.

sources.title: Presidencia Uruguay, Ley N° 18.589 de fecha 18/09/2009
sources.note: Official law record declaring every 11 April the Day of the Charrúa Nation and Indigenous Identity.

sources.title: José Ignacio Gomeza Gómez, Memorias en disputa. Usos, relatos y debates en torno a las acciones de Estado contra el pueblo charrúa en Uruguay
sources.note: Journal pages 4 to 6: family separation and imposed servitude after state violence; pages 17 to 21, especially 20 to 21: organizations, memories restricted to private settings, transmission in family settings, associations, and networks of affective or political sociability, followed by entry into public debate.

sources.title: Consejo de la Nación Charrúa, official site
sources.note: Community-controlled source checked 3 October 2026: organization created in 2005, multiple Uruguayan communities, living-community slogans, twentieth anniversary, and itinerant intercultural school announcement. Dedicated chiefly to living continuity.

sources.title: Argentina, Instituto Nacional de Asuntos Indígenas, Resolución 881 / 2013, COMUNIDAD NAYBU
sources.note: Official page heading “COMUNIDAD NAYBU,” Article 1, and record dates: legal personality for the Naybu community of the Charrúa people in rural Colonia Federal, Entre Ríos; sanctioned 9 October 2013 and published 3 April 2014.

sources.title: Institución Nacional de Derechos Humanos, Día Internacional de la Mujer Indígena
sources.note: Official 4 September 2020 page: 2011 ancestry figures, named organizations, women’s cultural and socio-educational work, and access concerns. Figures are Indigenous, not specifically Charrúa.

sources.title: Institución Nacional de Derechos Humanos, Identidad y cultura indígena en Uruguay
sources.note: Official 24 April 2025 report: Charrúa and Chaná film forum, Basquadé Inchalá participation, collaborative creative process, and planned circulation in educational centers.

sources.title: Emilia Martínez Rojo et al., Salud y Territorio en la zona norte de Rocha, Uruguay
sources.note: PDF section “2. Bañados del Este de Rocha: una mirada histórica,” subsections “Cerritos de Indios” and “Los cerritos de indios en India Muerta,” especially paragraphs beginning “Dentro de los sitios analizados...” and “Se trata de una forma...”: nine García Ricci mounds, age and height ranges, earth architecture, nearby and burned soil, animal and fish bones, dog remains, pottery, stone-tool debris, and hearth remains.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología, Paneles Exposición Educativa Arqueología
sources.note: Panels headed “TECNOLOGÍA CERÁMICA,” especially “EL HALLAZGO DE CERÁMICA EN SITIOS PREHISTÓRICOS DEL URUGUAY Y LA INFORMACIÓN QUE NOS BRINDA” and “POSIBLES USOS DE LA CERÁMICA”: more than 3,000 years of pottery, manufacture, domestic soot, symbolic forms, and funerary urns; the panels do not attribute these examples to named Charrúa people.

sources.title: Diego Suárez, Arqueología experimental y Paleoetnobotánica de los constructores de cerritos del Este del Uruguay: una aproximación a partir del registro macrobotánico del sitio CH2D01
sources.note: Udelar repository abstract, labelled “dc.description.abstract”: CH2D01 late-Holocene chronology, flotation and experimental methods, 840 plant charcoals, identified plant taxa, the role of Butiá and Pindó palms, and wood fuel.

sources.title: Bracco and colleagues, El fuego, los hornos de tierra y la elevación de los montículos de la cuenca de la Laguna Merín
sources.note: Udelar repository abstract, lines 14 to 33, for the 2021 peer-reviewed study: repeated earth ovens, possible plant processing, and secular debris accumulation as a mound-formation hypothesis.

sources.title: Erbig and Latini, Across Archival Limits: Colonial Records, Changing Ethnonyms, and Geographies of Knowledge
sources.note: PDF pages 1 and 11 to 14, journal pages 249 and 259 to 262: colonial archives are geographically partial; ethnonyms shifted; Charrúa first appears in a 1527 account; catchall labels obscured distinct tolderías and kin networks.

sources.title: Juan Justino da Rosa, Historiografía lingüística del Río de la Plata: las lenguas indígenas de la Banda Oriental
sources.note: PDF pages 1 to 2 and 5 to 9, journal pages 131 to 140: sparse linguistic evidence, uncertain classifications, conflation of language, ethnicity, and nation, and the late scholarly history of Charrúa word lists.
